# 2 Maccabees Chapter 6 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 6 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_006_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Not long after this, the king sent an Athenian elder to compel the Jews to abandon the laws of their ancestors and no longer to live in accordance with the laws of God,

**2** and also to defile the temple in Jerusalem and to rename it after Olympian Zeus, and to rename the one on Mount Gerizim after Zeus-Hospitius, as the inhabitants of that place had requested.

**3** Harsh and utterly grievous was the oppression that came.

**4** For the temple was filled with debauchery and carousing by the Gentiles, who consorted with prostitutes and had intercourse with women within the sacred precincts, and who brought into the holy place things that were not permitted.

**5** The altar was piled with unlawful offerings that the law forbade.

**6** A person could neither keep the sabbath nor observe the traditional festivals, nor so much as confess to being a Jew.

**7** On the king's monthly birthday, the Jews were driven by harsh compulsion to partake of the sacrifices. When the feast of Dionysus came, they were compelled to walk in procession in honor of Dionysus, wearing garlands of ivy.

**8** A decree went out at the instigation of Ptolemy to the neighboring Greek cities, ordering that they follow the same policy toward the Jews and compel them to partake of the sacrifices,

**9** and to put to death those who did not consent to adopt Greek customs. The scale of the present misery was therefore plain to see.

**10** For two women were brought in who had circumcised their children. These women were paraded through the city with their infants hanging at their breasts, and then were hurled headlong from the city wall.

**11** Others who had gathered in nearby caves to observe the sabbath in secret were denounced to Philip, and were all burned together, because in their reverence for the holiness of the day they had refused to defend themselves.

**12** Now I urge those who read this book not to be dismayed by these calamities, but to recognize that these punishments were not intended to destroy our people but to discipline them.

**13** For it is a mark of great favor that the impious are not left long undisturbed but are immediately punished.

**14** In the case of other nations, the Sovereign Lord waits patiently until they have reached the full measure of their sins before he punishes them; but with us he has decided to act differently,

**15** so that he may not have to take vengeance on us later when our sins have reached their full extent.

**16** Therefore he never withdraws his mercy from us. Although he disciplines us with calamity, he does not abandon his own people.

**17** Let this much serve as a reminder; after a few words we must continue with the narrative.

**18** Eleazar, one of the chief scribes, a man of advanced years and distinguished bearing, was being forced to open his mouth and eat pork.

**19** But he, preferring an honorable death to a life of defilement, went forward to the instrument of torture of his own accord, spitting out the pork,

**20** as those ought to do who have the resolve to refuse food that it is wrong to taste, even for the love of life.

**21** Those who were in charge of that unlawful sacrifice, because of their long acquaintance with the man, took him aside and privately urged him to bring meat that was lawful for him to eat, and to pretend that he was eating the flesh of the sacrificial meal as required by the king,

**22** so that by doing this he might be saved from death, and that for the sake of their old friendship with him they might treat him with some consideration.

**23** But he, making a decision worthy of his years and the dignity of old age and the distinguished gray hairs he had attained, and worthy of his excellent conduct from childhood, and most of all of the holy laws ordained by God — he answered without hesitation, telling them to send him to Hades at once.

**24** "Such a pretense," he said, "is not fitting for a man of our time of life. It might lead many of the young to think that Eleazar in his ninetieth year has gone over to an alien religion,

**25** and through my deceit, for the sake of clinging to this brief life a little longer, I would bring defilement and stain upon my old age.

**26** Even if for the present I were to escape human punishment, whether I live or die I cannot escape the hands of the Almighty.

**27** Therefore, by bravely giving up my life right now, I shall show myself worthy of my old age,

**28** and leave to the young a noble example of how to die willingly and courageously for the sake of the revered and holy laws."

**29** When he had said this, he went straight to the instrument of torture.

**30** And those who just before had been treating him with goodwill now turned to hostility toward him, because the words he had spoken seemed to them sheer madness.

**31** When he was on the point of dying from the blows, he groaned and said: "It is clear to the LORD in his holy knowledge that, though I could have been saved from death, I am suffering terrible pain in my body from the blows, but in my soul I am content to endure this because of my fear of him."

**32** So the man died in this manner, leaving by his death not only a noble example but also a memorial of virtue — not only for young people but for the whole nation.
